abstract: Advances in large-molecule delivery across the blood-brain barrier (BBB) by targeting receptors such as transferrin receptor (TfR) or CD98 heavy chain (CD98hc) are shifting the focus from restricted parenchymal access toward brain exposure profiles tailored to therapeutic needs. However, brain concentrations offer only partial insight into delivery mechanisms, as they reflect the net balance of two dynamic processes: flux of molecules entering and leaving the brain, here termed brain uptake and brain clearance, respectively. Here, we establish a generalizable experimental and mathematical modeling framework to resolve these opposing fluxes and demonstrate its application using pharmacokinetic (PK) data from Fc-engineered antibody transport vehicles (ATVs) targeting TfR or CD98hc in humanized knock-in mouse models. First, to directly estimate brain clearance, we engineered anti-ATV antibodies that selectively bind the TV patch to block receptor-mediated brain uptake in vivo. Integrating these measurements with a mechanistic PK model, we then reconstructed brain fluxes of ATV molecules over time across a broad range of receptor affinities. Results demonstrated that TfR-targeting promotes rapid, affinity-dependent brain uptake accompanied by comparatively rapid brain clearance, whereas CD98hc-targeting results in slower brain uptake and prolonged retention. Extending this framework to dual TfR/CD98hc-targeting ATVs suggested that higher observed brain exposure relative to single-receptor formats does not necessarily translate to greater brain delivery: increased exposure was predicted to arise primarily from reduced brain clearance, associated with CD98hc-mediated retention, rather than enhanced uptake through dual-receptor engagement. Together, these results establish a quantitative basis for resolving brain fluxes and engineering brain-targeted biologics for desired therapeutic outcomes.
